title: Charles de Foucauld
hookLine: a soldier turned hermit lives among the Tuareg in the Sahara as a brother to all

lines: AN OFFICER WITH DEBTS AND PARTIES.
cards: A young French cavalry officer throws parties, runs up debts, and gets disciplined for bringing a mistress along on a posting to North Africa. Faith means nothing to him.
Years later the same man lives in a small hut deep in the Sahara, with a notebook of words in the language of the Tuareg, the desert people around him, and a chapel the size of a closet.
He doesn't preach on street corners or run a school. Mostly, he's just there, with his door open.

teach.b: Back in the faith as a young man, Charles de Foucauld looked for the plainest life he could find. He tried a monastery, and left it for something even smaller.
What drew him was the part of Jesus's life the Gospels barely describe: the quiet years in Nazareth. Luke gives them two verses.

In the King James Bible: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them." No sermons, no miracles, just a household. That hidden life, Foucauld decided, was a way to follow Jesus too.
So he went into the desert to be a neighbor. He learned Tuareg well enough to gather their poems and write down their words. He gave out medicine and grain and sat with whoever came by.
He wrote that he wanted everyone around him, Christian, Muslim, Jewish or anyone else, to see him as a brother, a universal brother, and he called his little house the fraternity.
In Luke, a lawyer asks Jesus who his neighbor is.
Jesus tells of a Samaritan who stops for a beaten stranger, then turns the question around: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?"
Some readers hear Foucauld's life as an answer. He built no large church. He died at his own door during a raid.
But others later formed communities inspired by him, small groups who live and work among the poor, and the Catholic Church has named him a saint.
This week: soup, soap and salvation in the East End. Hudson Taylor in Chinese clothes. Amy Carmichael's love that costs.
The spring at the grotto. Small things, great love. We lepers.
And a brother in the desert. Seven stories, one direction: closer.

how: Small communities of laypeople, priests and religious sisters inspired by Charles de Foucauld live simply among poor neighbors, working ordinary jobs and keeping a time of quiet prayer each day.

games.q: you've come back to faith and want to follow Jesus as closely as you can. which part of his life do you copy?
o: the preaching tours, crowds and all.
the time alone in the wilderness.
games.why: Foucauld chose Nazareth: the hidden years Luke sums up in two short verses. he lived as a plain neighbor among the Tuareg.

practice: Picture one person near you who isn't family and isn't quite a friend: a coworker, a neighbor, the person who cleans your building. Foucauld's whole method was attention: a language learned, a door open, time given.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, give them a minute of that attention.
